#!/bin/bash
# Run cargo against one crustify prebuild of libgit2, instrumenting Rust to match.
#
#   crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh <variant> <cargo subcommand> [args...]
#
# <variant> is a `variants` key of crustify/artifacts/build.json: plain, coverage, asan-ubsan,
# tsan or bsan. Each variant uses its own target dir under target/.
# The safe crate's build script, in campaign mode, links the variant's static archive (its
# `static` in build.json) into each test binary, so the C runs under the instrumentation the
# Rust is built with here, one runtime serving both. Set CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR to a private build
# of the variant, which carries the same archive, to link it instead of the shared one.
set -euo pipefail
variant=${1:?usage: cargo-variant.sh <variant> <cargo subcommand> [args...]}
shift
here=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)
host=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
export CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=$variant
export CARGO_TARGET_DIR=${CARGO_TARGET_DIR:-$here/target/$variant}
# pcre2-sys links the variant's side-campaign PCRE2, the one libgit2's C links, rather than
# building its vendored copy, which would shadow it in every test binary. The side campaigns'
# clones sit where the variant's build found their installs, beside the repository whose
# crustify/builds holds it (build.json's configure takes them from `$PWD/../../../..` in
# crustify/builds/<variant>): resolved physically through crustify/builds, which a worktree or
# a gate snapshot links to that repository's, so that every checkout finds the same ones.
side=$(realpath -m "$here/crustify/builds/$variant/../../../..")
export PKG_CONFIG_PATH="$side/pcre2-bindings/crustify/builds/$variant/install/lib/pkgconfig${PKG_CONFIG_PATH:+:$PKG_CONFIG_PATH}"
cd "$here"
# The nightly the workspace pins, for the sanitizers that need it.
nightly=$(sed -n 's/^nightly = "\(.*\)"$/\1/p' Cargo.toml)
# Cargo's own flags must come before a `--`, which hands the rest to the test binaries.
pre=() post=()
for arg in "$@"; do
  if [ ${#post[@]} -gt 0 ] || [ "$arg" = -- ]; then post+=("$arg"); else pre+=("$arg"); fi
done
case $variant in
  plain)
    exec cargo "$@" ;;
  coverage)
    # Source-based coverage on the pinned nightly, against the variant's clang-instrumented C,
    # which each test binary links statically, so that rustc's profiler runtime counts both;
    # crustify/scripts/coverage/ measures the suites as the testing spec's Coverage section does.
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -C instrument-coverage"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -C instrument-coverage"
    export LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=${LLVM_PROFILE_FILE:-$CARGO_TARGET_DIR/profraw/%p-%m.profraw}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  asan-ubsan)
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=address -Cforce-frame-pointers=yes"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=address"
    export ASAN_OPTIONS=${ASAN_OPTIONS:-detect_leaks=1:abort_on_error=1}
    export UBSAN_OPTIONS=${UBSAN_OPTIONS:-print_stacktrace=1:halt_on_error=1}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  tsan)
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=thread"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=thread"
    # glibc's tzset locks what TSan cannot see: see tsan.supp.
    export TSAN_OPTIONS=${TSAN_OPTIONS:-halt_on_error=1:suppressions=$here/crustify/scripts/tsan.supp}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" -Zbuild-std --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  bsan)
    # trybuild's nested cargo build does not finish under BorrowSanitizer, and the
    # compile-fail suite is a compile-time check the plain variant already runs.
    # Under parallel test threads BorrowSanitizer's GC can take longer than its default
    # 10 s hang threshold to bring every thread to a safepoint, and then aborts; give it
    # 120 s rather than serialize the tests.
    export BSAN_OPTIONS=${BSAN_OPTIONS:-gc_hang_threshold_ms=120000}
    if [ "${1:-}" = test ]; then
      case " $* " in
        *" -- "*) exec cargo bsan "$@" --skip compile_fail ;;
        *) exec cargo bsan "$@" -- --skip compile_fail ;;
      esac
    fi
    exec cargo bsan "$@" ;;
  *)
    echo "unknown variant: $variant" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac

1	//! `src/cli/opt.c`: the command-line argument parser of the `git2` CLI (`src/cli/opt.h`),
2	//! ported to Rust.
3	//!
4	//! The header's enums are native Rust: [`Kind`] and [`Status`] are closed enums, whose
5	//! discriminants stay C's values while the CLI's remaining C, its `cmd_*.c` spec tables,
6	//! `opt_usage.c` and `common.c`, uses their constants, and [`Usage`] and [`ParseFlags`] are
7	//! bit sets, which that C combines with `|`. `opt.h` keeps the C definitions for that C:
8	//! the two are not linked.
9	//!
10	//! The parser's helpers are native Rust too: [`Kind::is_option`], `opt.c`'s
11	//! `spec_is_option_type`, and [`uses_gnu_style`], its `support_gnu_style`, and the routines
12	//! through which the parser finds the spec an argument selects, steps over a choice and checks
13	//! the required arguments. No C outside `opt.c` reaches them, so none is exported.
14	//!
15	//! # Its entry points
16	//!
17	//! [`Parser::new`] (`cli_opt_parser_init`) sets a parser up and [`ParserMut::parse_next`]
18	//! (`cli_opt_parser_next`) parses its arguments one by one, reordering them GNU style where it
19	//! was asked to; [`parse`] (`cli_opt_parse`) parses a whole command line and checks its required
20	//! arguments, and [`for_each`] (`cli_opt_foreach`) calls a [`ForeachCallbackFn`] with each
21	//! outcome, which a Rust closure or, through the export, `common.c`'s C function implements.
22	//! [`OptRef::write_status`] (`cli_opt_status_fprint`) describes an outcome, as the CLI shows it on
23	//! its standard error. The CLI's remaining C calls all five: `main.c` sets a parser up, steps it
24	//! and describes its failures, each `cmd_*.c` parses its own arguments, `common.c` reads the
25	//! configuration options, and `opt_usage.c` describes failures. So each has an export, compiled
26	//! under the module's export feature, `ffi-export-src-cli-opt-c`, which stays off until the
27	//! module switches from C.
28	//!
29	//! The parser corrects the C's defects, each
30	//! documented on the routine that departs: it reads no string past its end, nor through a null
31	//! pointer, and keeps any number of the specs a parse gives, where the C writes past a stack
32	//! array of one per argument; an unknown option ends its bundle; and GNU-style reordering moves
33	//! nothing after a literal `--`, and loses no bare argument before an option whose value is
34	//! optional.
35	//!
36	//! # The parser's structs
37	//!
38	//! The header's three structs keep their C layouts, which that C builds and reads in place:
39	//! its commands define their spec tables as `const cli_opt_spec[]` arrays, ended by a zeroed
40	//! spec, with each spec's `value` pointing at the command's own variable, and hold a
41	//! `cli_opt` and, in `main.c`, a `cli_opt_parser` on their stacks. Rust reaches them as
42	//! layouts with borrowed handles, until their `port/layout` stages give them native ones:
43	//!
44	//! - [`Spec`] (`cli_opt_spec`) describes one option or argument: its [`Kind`] with the variable a
45	//!   parse writes, as one [`Target`], its long name, its one-character alias, its switch value, its
46	//!   [`Usage`], and the value name and help text usage shows. A [`SpecTable`] is a run of specs
47	//!   ended by a zeroed one, as C passes them.
48	//! - [`Opt`] (`cli_opt`) is the outcome of parsing one argument: its [`Status`], the spec it
49	//!   matched, the argument and its value as they were given, and how many arguments an
50	//!   [`Kind::Args`] spec took.
51	//! - [`Parser`] (`cli_opt_parser`) is the parser's state over a spec table and an argument array:
52	//!   its [`ParseFlags`], its position, and whether it still has to reorder the arguments GNU style.
53	//!   [`Parser::new`] sets one up.
54	//!
55	//! Nothing here is owned: a parser, an outcome and a spec borrow their spec table, their
56	//! arguments and their spec's variables, which their caller keeps, and C never frees any of
57	//! them. Each of the three carries that borrow as `'p`, in which it is invariant, so that a
58	//! parse only stores into a variable, or hands out an argument, that lives as long as
59	//! everything that may read it. An argument is an [`Arg`], a borrowed C string; a variable a
60	//! parse writes is a [`Cell`](core::cell::Cell), or an [`ArgsSlot`] for the remaining
61	//! arguments, since several specs may share one, as switches multiplexing one mode do. C
62	//! parses on the thread that holds them, so none of them is `Send` or `Sync`.
63	
64	use core::cell::Cell;
65	use core::ffi::{CStr, c_int};
66	use core::num::NonZero;
67	use core::ops::{BitAnd, BitAndAssign, BitOr, BitOrAssign, ControlFlow};
68	use core::{fmt, ptr};
69	use std::io;
70	
71	pub use ffi_import::{
72	    Arg, ForeachCallbackFn, Opt, OptMut, OptRef, Parser, ParserMut, ParserRef, Spec, SpecMut,
73	    SpecRef, SpecTable,
74	};
75	use ffibox::{CRefSeam, CZeroable};
76	
77	/// The kind of command-line argument an option spec parses.
78	///
79	/// Its discriminants are C's values, the integer form through which the spec tables of the
80	/// CLI's remaining C pass it, until its `port/layout` removes them.
81	///
82	/// Replaces `enm::cli_opt_type_t`
83	#[doc(alias = "cli_opt_type_t")]
84	#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
85	#[repr(u32)]
86	pub enum Kind {
87	    /// No argument: the kind of the zeroed spec that ends a C spec table, which no
88	    /// argument matches.
89	    ///
90	    /// Replaces `enm::CLI_OPT_TYPE_NONE`
91	    #[doc(alias = "CLI_OPT_TYPE_NONE")]
92	    None = 0,
93	    /// An option that sets its value to true when given, as `--debug`, and to false when
94	    /// given with the implicit `no-` prefix, as `--no-debug`.
95	    ///
96	    /// Replaces `enm::CLI_OPT_TYPE_BOOL`
97	    #[doc(alias = "CLI_OPT_TYPE_BOOL")]
98	    Bool = 1,
99	    /// An option that sets its value to the spec's switch value when given, with no implicit
100	    /// negation: several switches may share one value to select a mode, as `--read` and
101	    /// `--write`.
102	    ///
103	    /// Replaces `enm::CLI_OPT_TYPE_SWITCH`
104	    #[doc(alias = "CLI_OPT_TYPE_SWITCH")]
105	    Switch = 2,
106	    /// An option that adds the spec's switch value to its value each time it is given, as
107	    /// `-vvv` for a verbosity of 3.
108	    ///
109	    /// Replaces `enm::CLI_OPT_TYPE_ACCUMULATOR`
110	    #[doc(alias = "CLI_OPT_TYPE_ACCUMULATOR")]
111	    Accumulator = 3,
112	    /// An option that takes a value: `-n value`, `-nvalue`, `--name value` or
113	    /// `--name=value`.
114	    ///
115	    /// Replaces `enm::CLI_OPT_TYPE_VALUE`
116	    #[doc(alias = "CLI_OPT_TYPE_VALUE")]
117	    Value = 4,
118	    /// The bare `--` after which every argument is literal, even one that looks like an
119	    /// option, as the `-rf` of `program -- -rf`.
120	    ///
121	    /// Replaces `enm::CLI_OPT_TYPE_LITERAL`
122	    #[doc(alias = "CLI_OPT_TYPE_LITERAL")]
123	    Literal = 5,
124	    /// A single argument that is not an option: once the options are exhausted, bare
125	    /// arguments match the argument specs in the order they are specified.
126	    ///
127	    /// Replaces `enm::CLI_OPT_TYPE_ARG`
128	    #[doc(alias = "CLI_OPT_TYPE_ARG")]
129	    Arg = 6,
130	    /// The remaining arguments, as a list, such as several paths.
131	    ///
132	    /// Replaces `enm::CLI_OPT_TYPE_ARGS`
133	    #[doc(alias = "CLI_OPT_TYPE_ARGS")]
134	    Args = 7,
135	}
136	
137	impl Kind {
138	    /// The kind whose C value is `raw`, or `None` for a value `opt.h` does not name.
139	    pub(crate) const fn from_raw(raw: u32) -> Option<Self> {
140	        match raw {
141	            0 => Some(Self::None),
142	            1 => Some(Self::Bool),
143	            2 => Some(Self::Switch),
144	            3 => Some(Self::Accumulator),
145	            4 => Some(Self::Value),
146	            5 => Some(Self::Literal),
147	            6 => Some(Self::Arg),
148	            7 => Some(Self::Args),
149	            _ => None,
150	        }
151	    }
152	
153	    /// The C value of the kind.
154	    pub(crate) const fn raw(self) -> u32 {
155	        self as u32
156	    }
157	}
158	
159	/// How an option spec is parsed and shown in usage: a set of flags, any combination of
160	/// which is valid.
161	///
162	/// The bits of [`from_bits_retain`](Self::from_bits_retain) that no constant names are kept,
163	/// as C keeps them in a spec's `usage`.
164	///
165	/// Replaces `enm::cli_opt_usage_t`
166	#[doc(alias = "cli_opt_usage_t")]
167	#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, Default, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
168	#[repr(transparent)]
169	pub struct Usage(u32);
170	
171	impl Usage {
172	    /// The argument is a choice with the spec before it: when that spec is `-f` and this one
173	    /// `-b`, one of `-f` or `-b` may be given.

---
name: accounting
description: "The dashboard, its cells, the runs' records and transcripts, and how cost and time are derived. Read before filling dashboard cells or collecting a run's records."
---

# Accounting

What a campaign records about its own work: the dashboard, the runs' records and
transcripts its figures come from, and how cost and time are derived from them.

## 1. The dashboard

The dashboard, `crustify/artifacts/dashboard.md` unless the settings name another, is the
campaign's record of what each planner run, batch, wave and module did and cost. It is
filled from `templates/translate/dashboard.template.md`, an audit's from
`templates/audit/dashboard.template.md`, and keeps the template's format exactly.
When an adopted Crustify change adds a table or a column to the template, it is
added to the dashboard on the working branch before the next batch launches: a batch
fills the rows of the tables in place, and never adds one.

It is tracked in the campaign's tree, so every agent's worktree holds a copy, and it is
filled as the work lands rather than at the end. Each figure is measured once, where it is
produced: no suite or scan is rerun only to record one.

## 2. Cells

The dashboard's cells fall into three kinds, by when their figures can be known.

### 2.1 Landing cells

The cells measured on the tree a landing commits:

- for a batch, under the route its items' `kind` selects, as
  [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Routes section gives it: its rows
  in that route's `Batches`, tests, `Batches: safety audit` and `Batches: API stability` tables, and for a review batch in
  `Batches — review: PoC + reports`, each placed in module, wave and batch order under
  its `pass`, and for a module pass, which spans both routes, in `Module passes`; those
  tables' `Σ` rows; and the `Coverage stats` table and the Overview's LoC
  line;
- for a planner run, its row in `Planning`, but for its usage cells.

They are filled in the landing's last commit, and measured against the integration branch
tip it was rebased onto: coverage as [`testing-builds`](../../verification/testing/builds/SKILL.md)'s Coverage section measures
it, the safety audit columns as the changes in the dashboard's Safety audit metrics, and
the API stability columns as the changes to the API of the landing's items are classified. A
rebase that conflicts in the dashboard keeps every row both sides added, and the landing's
cells, `Σ` rows included, are measured again where the gates its rebase reruns cover them;
the others stand as measured on the batch's base.

An integration merge, and any merge of one branch into another, keeps every row both
sides added, and settles the rest so: an additive `Σ` cell is the sum over the merged
rows, ours plus theirs less the merge base's, and so are the Overview's `Rust LoC`
figures; a usage `Σ` cell, its per-unit cells included, sums only the rows that carry
usage, so that it is filled again with theirs; a coverage `Σ` cell, and the Overview's
`C LoC`, are the later landing's; and `Coverage stats` takes the merged suites' counts,
with the later landing's percentages until a gate measures the merged tree, which the
merge commit's message says. A table or section the template holds once is kept once,
with the rows of every copy, whether or not the merge conflicts there, and the merged
dashboard is checked for repeated headings before it is committed.

### 2.2 Usage cells

The cells known only once an agent has ended, from its usage: its cost, tokens and wall,
the per-unit costs derived from them, and their `Σ` cells. A batch's are filled on the
working branch once its row is there, once its module is integrated, as
[`versioning`](../versioning/SKILL.md) describes, or, for a port's later-stage batch, which
runs after its module's switch, once its wave is promoted. A planner run's are filled once the run is
promoted. A batch run more than once costs the sum of its runs.

### 2.3 Campaign cells

The cells that span agents: the `Module stats` table, the Overview's branch line and
test baseline, and the `Settings` lines. A module's row and the branch line are filled
when the module is integrated, and a port's module row again as each of its later-stage
waves is promoted, the baseline once it is recorded, and the `Settings` lines,
with a Notes entry, whenever a settings change is applied.

### 2.4 Side campaign cells

A side campaign keeps its own dashboard, in its own repository, and its figures are
measured there. The parent's `Side campaigns` table copies them, one row per wrapper, as
they stand at the commit the parent pins, and the `side campaigns` row of `Module stats`
sums the rows, so that the parent's `Σ campaign` covers what its side campaigns cost. A
wrapper's row is filled each time the parent's pin moves, and its `shipped at` cell when
the wrapper ships the commit the parent pins. A side campaign that serves several parents
appears in each, with the figures as of each one's pin.

An audit's dashboard follows the same kinds over its own tables.

## 3. Records

Every run's `task.json` records how its agent ran: its backend, billing, model proxy and
the arguments its CLI was given, and, once it starts, its `session_id`, which ties the run
to its session. The session's transcript, which its CLI keeps by session id, is the
agent's full log and the source of its accounting. An agent spawned as a subagent of
another session has no session of its own: its session id is `agent-<agent id>`, the
name its host gives its transcript, under the spawning session's `subagents/`.

A transcript is copied into crustify's home, as `transcripts/<session id>.jsonl`, as soon
as its agent ends, because the CLIs move and prune their own files. Its usage is derived
from the copy, as [`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) describes, with the backend and model proxy its
`task.json` names.

An evolution review is a run like any other: its `task.json` sits in its artifact dir, and
its transcript is collected and priced the same way, its cost counted with the sessions that
orchestrate the campaign and recorded, with its tokens and wall time, in its proposal's
Review section, so that what each review bought can be weighed against its cost.

The sessions that orchestrate the campaign are collected the same way: at the start of each session, the
transcripts of the sessions before it. A resumed session keeps its id while its transcript
grows: its transcript is copied again after each run, replacing the earlier copy. The
records, transcripts and rates stay in crustify's home.

## 4. Cost and time

A run's cost and tokens are its usage's `total.cost_usd` and `total.tokens`, as
[`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) derives them from its transcript. The computed cost is used, never a provider-reported
dollar total; under subscription billing it is the API-equivalent cost.

An agent's wall time is its usage's interval. A wave's runs from its first batch's
launch through its final review and regression gates, a review wave's in an audit through
its landing, and a module's from its first launch through its final gate.

## Legend

- `module` / `wave` / `batch` — the batch's place in `schedule.json`: its wave's module and
  the wave and batch indices
- `objective` — `wrap` or `port`; `pass` — `first` for a translation batch, `review` for a
  review batch; `Σ first` / `Σ review` total each pass apart
- `types` / `symbols` / `fields` — the batch's scheduled units (callbacks count as
  symbols) and its types' assigned field accessors; a review row counts what it reviewed
- `$` / `tokens` / `wall` — the agent's computed cost (API-equivalent under
  subscription), its tokens in millions as `crustify usage` reports them, and its elapsed
  time, C rebuild included; `$/<unit>` divides `$` by the row's units
- `+LoC` — the landing's Rust insertions/deletions; `loc` — its `.rs` insertions
- `cov (C/Rust)` — line coverage after the landing, all test workloads in one run: C over
  the link unit's TUs, Rust over non-test sources; a `Σ` cell is the pass's last landing
- `+UB safe tests` … `+unit tests` — the tests the landing added, with its C/Rust coverage
  change in pp
- `+lifecycle` … `+misc`, `total` — the reports a review batch filed, by kind
- safety audit columns — the Safety audit's metrics, as a landing changed them
- API stability columns — the landing's items by how `ffimap api` classifies their consumer-facing API against its base: `kept`, `extended`, `changed`, `removed`, `new`, and `→Replaces` for the anchors a port moved; `unattributed` the crate's public items no anchor reaches, by module; `reasons` the changed and removed items with the reason the batch recorded
- `cost` / `review cost` / `total` — a module's translation, review and combined cost;
  `module wall` — first launch to final gate; `Σ recorded agents` leaves the assistant
  out, `Σ campaign` adds it, without per-unit cells
- `UB safe tests` … `Unit tests` — `#[test]` functions per suite, each with the coverage of
  running it alone; `Total tests` — all four, whose coverage is one joint run's union,
  never the sum
- `total`, `ported` and `wrapped` types and symbols — the scheduled public-API units, and
  those with a `Replaces:` or a `Wraps:` anchor at the tip; `share` is of the total

input.command: cat /crustify-rs/crustify/skills/rust/porting/SKILL.md /crustify-rs/crustify/skills/rust/porting/symbols/SKILL.md | grep -v '^$'

content.content:
---
name: porting
description: "How a scheduled C item is reimplemented in safe Rust: its native API, its later stages, the FFI boundary and its exports, and the routes porting-types and porting-symbols give types and symbols. Read before porting any item, and when reviewing ports."
---
# Porting
How a scheduled C item is reimplemented in safe Rust. A port starts from the item's
analysis, as [`analysis`](../analysis/SKILL.md) describes, and keeps C interoperability
and observable behaviour for as long as C consumes the item. A type takes the type route,
for structs, unions, enums and typedefs, as [`porting-types`](types/SKILL.md) describes; a
symbol the symbol route, for functions, globals, function pointers, static inline functions
and macros, as [`porting-symbols`](symbols/SKILL.md) describes.
A port gives an item its native safe API at once, and that API does not change after it.
An item the remaining C still uses keeps a C form behind it, its C layout, its storage in
C's allocator, its export or its integer values, so that the C keeps working while its
Rust consumers stay agnostic of which form implements it. The later stages its kind
describes below migrate that form to Rust, part by part, once the switches that free
it have landed, as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages
section schedules them. An item no C uses is native in its API and its implementation from
its port.
A later stage changes the item and the code inside the crate that reaches its C form, in
its module's unsafe regions, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Unsafe regions
section describes, never the safe API its consumers use, and keeps the item's tests
passing. A stage that moves state out of C, a lock or a handle a type held in its C layout,
or memory C's allocator held, moves its uses onto the standard library where
[`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section lets it.
## 1. FFI boundary
`binding`'s Safe boundary section applies to a port unchanged. When a wrapper of the item
already exists, because a module that ran before needed it, the port keeps that wrapper's
safe API and replaces only what is behind it, so that its consumers do not change, as do
its later stages. A standard-library operation is used directly when it is equivalent and
no C-interoperability requirement remains, an out-of-tree library's entity included, as
`binding`'s Safe boundary section describes.
While C consumers remain, a ported item is re-exported to C as the
[conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Exports section describes:
- The raw gateway, its module's `ffi_export` region, reconstructs safe wrappers and calls
  the native function.
- The gateway is compiled only under its module's export feature, which stays off until
  the module switches, so that the exports never collide with the C they replace.
- At the switch, the Rust static library is linked in place of the TU through the actual
  build system, without assuming link mechanics, and the TU is deleted, as
  [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes.
---
name: porting-symbols
description: "How a scheduled C symbol is reimplemented in safe Rust, porting's symbol route: functions and their exports, globals, function pointers, static inline functions and macros, each with its later stages. Read before porting any symbol, and when reviewing ports."
---
# Porting symbols
How a scheduled C symbol is reimplemented in safe Rust: the symbol route, which follows
[`porting`](../SKILL.md)'s FFI boundary section and starts from
[`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s; the types it reaches are
[`porting-types`](../types/SKILL.md)'s.
A ported symbol's implementation is translated to safe, idiomatic Rust with its observable
behaviour preserved.
## 1. Functions
A ported function takes the safe API [`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Functions
section gives a function, or keeps its wrapper's, as [`porting`](../SKILL.md)'s FFI boundary section describes.
A function that remaining C calls or takes the address of is exported, as
[`porting`](../SKILL.md)'s FFI boundary section describes. Its gateway undoes what the safe API converted,
so that its C callers see what the C function did: it rebuilds the safe arguments from the
C ones, writes the out-parameters and buffers through the pointers C passed, and reports a
failure through the function's C error convention, its return and the error state the C
function set, `errno` included, which the Rust behind it never sets. A panic is caught at
the gateway and reported as a failure, or aborts where the function cannot fail: none
unwinds into C. A variadic function's export cannot be defined on stable Rust, so a shim
keeps its C signature, as [`bindgen`](../../bindgen/SKILL.md)'s shims are compiled, and calls
a fixed-arity export with the arguments it formats or unpacks. Its later stage, `port/unexport`, removes the
export, with the raw binding and the allowlist entry that reach it, once no remaining C
references it.
A lifecycle routine's port reimplements it behind the policy its type's port or wrap
wrote, which it repoints at the Rust routine, and writes no API of its own, as `binding-types`'
Lifecycle section has the symbol route skip what a type batch emitted. The last of its
type's own module's memory users to be ported moves its storage to Rust's allocator,
unless C of other modules still allocates or frees it raw, which leaves that move to its
`port/memory`.
## 2. Globals
A ported global takes the safe API [`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s
Globals section gives a global, or keeps its wrapper's. Rust holds its storage from its
port, beside its module's C, which keeps its own copy until the switch; from then on
the Rust's is the only one. A global that remaining C accesses
is exported, as a function is, and keeps the C layout and the synchronization protocol
those accesses rely on while it is. Its later stage, `port/unexport`, removes the export, as
a function's does, and its storage then takes a native form, as state moved out of C does.
A thread-local one cannot be defined for C on stable Rust, so a shim keeps its C definition,
as [`bindgen`](../../bindgen/SKILL.md)'s shims are compiled, until that stage. A global no
remaining C accesses is native from its port.
## 3. Function pointers
A ported function pointer keeps the safe callable type
[`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Function pointers section gives it, which is its API from its port: its Rust consumers, and
the ported code that calls it, use that type alone. While remaining C calls a function
pointer of its type or supplies one, its C form stays beneath it: the function-pointer type
of its raw binding, the trampolines through which a Rust closure reaches the C that calls
it, and the `unsafe` constructor through which a C function reaches Rust, passed to an
export, whose gateway builds the C variant from the function and the context it receives,
or stored where C wrote it. Its later stage, `port/unexport`, removes that C form, with the
raw binding and the allowlist entry that reach it, once no remaining C references it, as
[`scheduling`](../../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages section times it. A
function pointer no remaining C calls or supplies by its port is native in its
implementation too: its closure or trait alone.
A function pointer on the target's public API keeps its closure or trait through its
`port/unexport`, even when Rust alone implements it, so that the deferred public C API, as
[`conventions`](../../conventions/SKILL.md)'s Exports section describes, can let C
implement it again.
## 4. Static inline functions
A `static inline` function a header defines is internal API of the module the
decomposition gives it, and is ported as its other functions are. Its C callers expand its
body in their own TUs, so an export alone does not reach them: at the module's
switch, the header's definition is replaced by its prototype, and the remaining C
calls the Rust module's export, under the function's bare name, where it inlined the body.
<!-- TODO: cross-language LTO (`-Clinker-plugin-lto`, with a clang whose LLVM matches
rustc's) would inline the export back into its C callers. -->
## 5. Macros
A macro takes the Rust form [`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Macros section gives it,
which reaches the Rust items its expansion uses once they are ported. A macro a TU defines
goes with its TU. A macro a header defines, internal or public API that another module's C
may expand, also stays in its header for the remaining C, unexported, and its C and Rust
forms are not linked, beyond the Rust form's annotation. It keeps expanding where remaining C
invokes it, until its header goes with the last C file that includes it, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Principles section
describes: a type generator keeps minting the instances its remaining invocations define,
and what an expansion calls or accesses is reached as any remaining C reaches it, a
function or global Rust owns through its export, a type through its C layout. An
expansion site is a use by the function that holds it, so it holds back the later stages
of what it reaches, as [`scheduling`](../../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages
section counts its users.

---
name: conventions
description: "Naming, tree layout, anchors and test placement of the Rust a campaign generates. Read before writing, homing or reviewing generated Rust or tests."
---
# Crustify coding conventions
These are the shared, mechanical contracts of the code a campaign generates: how it is
named, where it sits, how it records what it translated and where its tests go. The
toolchain, edition, lints and formatting it is held to are [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s.
## 1. Naming
The workspace's lints enforce the standard Rust casing below, as [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s
Lints section describes.
The safe surface uses ordinary Rust naming: `snake_case` for functions, methods and
modules, `UpperCamelCase` for types and traits, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` for constants and
statics. A C name's library or owning-type prefix is dropped wherever the crate, module or
receiver already supplies it, and the idiomatic Rust term is preferred over a
transliterated C one. The filled anchor records the C name, so renaming costs no
traceability. Names that cross the language boundary keep their C-derived spelling, as
below.
### 1.1 Functions
A C function's raw binding is `sys::<name>`. Its safe wrapper is a free function homed in
the owning module, named by the rules above. When one C function has several valid
ownership contracts, each safe variant has a distinct, descriptive name.
### 1.2 Types
A wrapped C type is the layout-compatible newtype `Foo`, named by the rules above; its
shared and exclusive borrowed handles are `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`, and its sole and
counted owners `FooBox` and `FooArc`. A port keeps these names while what they name
changes, as [`porting-types`](../porting/types/SKILL.md)'s Structs section describes. A typedef that
names a type under another name, which its item lists among its `typedefs`, is a
`pub type` alias of the type's Rust form.
A function pointer a typedef declares is named after its typedef. One written inline is
named after the site that declares it, its holder's name followed by its own and `Fn`: a
field's `<Struct><Field>Fn`, a parameter's `<Function><Param>Fn`, a return's
`<Function>ReturnFn` and a global's `<Global>Fn`.
### 1.3 Shims
A callable macro shim is `crustify_<NAME>`.
### 1.4 Exports
Each ported module has one raw ABI gateway, its `ffi_export` region, as
[Unsafe regions](#21-unsafe-regions) describes, whose exports use `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] extern "C"` under the bare C names: the
module's functions and globals that C outside the module references, another module's TU
or a C test or executable that stays, the `static inline` functions its headers define
included. The exports serve that C, which reaches the module through them once it has
switched. A function or global only the module's own C references is not exported: that
C leaves the build with the module at its switch, and its callers are Rust from then
on; nor are static functions and static globals, which nothing outside their TU reaches.
The target's public C API, for C outside the target, is deferred: exports serve the
target's own remaining C alone, and that API is a layer of its own over the native Rust API,
added once the modules it covers are ported.
<!-- TODO: that layer, a C-compatible ABI over the ported public API, is not specified
yet. Until it is, a C consumer outside the target does not survive a port. -->
An export is removed, with the raw binding that reaches it, by its symbol's `port/unexport`,
after the switch that removes the last C that calls it, takes its address or
accesses it. A C test tied to the module that stays, using only its public API, does not
hold an export back: it checks the export while other C needs it, and leaves with it.
### 1.5 Export features
Each module's `ffi_export` is compiled only under the safe crate's Cargo feature
`ffi-export-<tu>`, with `<tu>` its translation unit's path below the C root, every character
that is not an ASCII letter or digit replaced by `-`. The feature is off until the module
switches, so that its exports never collide with the C they replace, and the switch
deletes it, its gateway compiling unconditionally from then on.
## 2. Crates, modules, and TUs
The Rust tree is the repository's own, as [`layout`](../../operations/layout/SKILL.md)'s Tree section lays it
out, all relative to the repository's root:
- `Cargo.toml` - the safe crate's manifest, which also declares the workspace.
- `src/lib.rs` - the safe crate's root, with one `cfg`-gated module per link unit.
- `src/<link-unit>/` - one sub-dir per link unit.
- `src/sys.rs` and `sys/<link-unit>/` - the raw bindings, one public module per link unit,
  laid out as [`bindgen`](../bindgen/SKILL.md) describes.
The safe crate is named after its repository, `<repo>-crustify`, as
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Repositories section names it:
a name crates.io leaves free, which tells it apart from the source's own Rust bindings,
such as `git2` for libgit2.
Within a link unit's sub-dir, the tree follows the module decomposition in `modules.json`
exactly, and preserves the C layout as far as the idiomatic organization of a Rust tree
allows:
- each module is one `.rs` file, at its translation unit's path below the C root with the
  `.rs` extension: its TU and the headers bundled with it have no files of their own,
  since Rust has no headers;
- a header module is one `<stem>_h.rs` file, at its header's path;
- the two modules of a split foundational TU share the TU's file;
- C directories become Rust modules: a directory's `.rs` file sits beside the directory,
  as `<dir>.rs` and `<dir>/`, and declares the modules within it, or is the module of a TU
  with the directory's name where there is one; `mod.rs` files are not used; and
- a file or directory name that is not a Rust identifier is sanitized, hyphens to
  underscores, and a Rust keyword takes a trailing underscore.
Where a C layout has no idiomatic Rust counterpart, the tree adapts it in the conventional
Rust way and keeps the C path recognizable. A batch names the `.rs` file each of its items
belongs in, as `src/<link-unit>/…/<file>.rs`. Entities sharing a
definition site co-home. A home may be shared across waves.
### 2.1 Unsafe regions
A module's unsafe code is confined to at most two inline child modules of its file, its
unsafe regions, so that the rest of the file, its native code, holds none:
- `mod ffi_import`: what the module reaches in C: its calls through the raw bindings, the C
  layouts it wraps with their handles and accessors, the owners and lifecycle policies over
  C's allocator, and the trampolines and contexts through which C calls a Rust closure
  back; and
- `mod ffi_export { use super::*; … }`: the gateway through which C reaches the module by
  symbol, as [Exports](#14-exports) describes, compiled only under its
  [export feature](#15-export-features).
Unsafe code is every `unsafe` block, `unsafe fn`, `unsafe impl`, `unsafe extern` block and
`#[unsafe(…)]` attribute, and every invocation of another crate's macro that expands to
one, such as one that mints a type over a C layout, which the compiler's `unsafe_code` lint does not
see. Outside the regions, only the raw bindings hold any. The regions take the lint back as
[`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Unsafe code section describes.
A region exposes to its module only what [`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary
section lets it expose, and the module re-exports the public items a region defines, as
`pub use ffi_import::{Foo, FooBox, FooMut, FooRef};`, so that their paths do not depend on
which side defines them. A type's inherent `impl` blocks may be split between the native
code and a region: each method is visible as its own visibility says, counted from the
module that holds its block, so that a region's private helpers stay hidden from the
native code.
A region exists only while it holds something. A wrap's items are in `ffi_import`. A port
writes its item in the native code, and keeps in the regions only the C form the item
keeps, as [`porting`](../porting/SKILL.md) describes; a wrapped item it ports leaves
`ffi_import` with its re-export. The later stages empty the regions part by part: an
item's C layout and C owners leave `ffi_import` with its `port/layout` and `port/memory`,
its export leaves `ffi_export` with its `port/unexport`. A module without either region is
native, and its file carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`.
## 3. Anchors
The Rust item that stands in for each C item is annotated, and those annotations are the
only record that an item was translated.
An annotation is two attributes on the same Rust item, a doc-comment anchor and a rustdoc
alias:
```rust
/// Wraps `fn::git_repository_open`
#[doc(alias = "git_repository_open")]
pub fn open(path: &Path) -> Result<RepositoryBox, Error> { … }
```
| anchor | meaning |
|---|---|
| ``/// Wraps `<kind>::<path>` `` | safe view over the FFI seam |
| ``/// Replaces `<kind>::<path>` `` | native Rust translation |
The anchor's path is a code span, in backticks, as rustdoc renders it and as the
workspace's `clippy::doc_markdown` lint requires of a path in a doc comment.
`<path>` names the item as its batch schedules it, and `<kind>` says what it is:
| kind | item |
|---|---|
| `fn` | a function |
| `st` | a struct |
| `un` | a union |
| `enm` | an enum, or one of its constants |
| `fnp` | a function pointer |
| `tdf` | a typedef: one of its own, or one an item lists among its `typedefs` |
| `fld` | a member of a struct or union |
| `glb` | a global |
| `mac` | a macro |
A path is made of names only: the names the source resolves the item by, outermost first,
separated by `.`, as the source language scopes them. A function, a type, an enum's
constant, a global, a typedef or a function pointer a typedef declares is its own name,
since C scopes a constant as it does its enum. A member is its struct's or union's path
followed by the member's name, and a member of a member continues the path, as
`fld::AVOption.default_val.i64`. A function pointer written inline is its declaring site's
path: a member's, `<function>.<param>` for a parameter, `<function>.return` for a return,
or a global's name. An element without a name adds no step to the paths of what it holds:
- an anonymous struct or union held by a named member is reached through that member, so
  its members are `fld::<path>.<member>.<inner>`;
- the members of an unnamed struct or union member, such as C11's anonymous members, are
  named as members of the type that holds it, as the source reaches them; and
- an array's elements are reached without an index, so the members of an array member's
  element type are `fld::<path>.<member>.<inner>`.
An element without a name has no annotation of its own. The Rust item that stands in for
it is annotated with the named member that holds it, or, when it is held by no name, with
each member it stands in for. A type declared inside another is named as its language
scopes it: a C struct tag has file scope, so a struct declared inside another is still
`st::<tag>`. An enum without a name has no annotation of its own, and its constants keep
theirs.
The alias is the bare `<path>`, without the backticks, so that a consumer who searches the
documentation for the source's name finds every item that stands in for it. The kind is
the anchor's alone: a label in the alias would no longer match that search.
### 3.1 What is annotated
The annotation goes on the public item a consumer uses in place of the C item, which is
not necessarily the item that makes the FFI call:
- a function: the function or method the public API exports, which a consumer imports
  instead of the FFI function. The private helper that makes the call, an `ffi_export`
  gateway and a test are not annotated.
- a lifecycle routine, raw, typed or string: the method of the public lifecycle trait the
  strategy implements, such as `CDrop::c_drop`, where it is handwritten, or the macro
  invocation that mints it, which passes the annotation to the method. Again, the method
  annotated need not be the one making the unsafe call.
- a type: the layout newtype that defines the FFI type, handwritten or minted by
  `define_ctype!`.
- a union: the tagged enum that stands in for it at every use.
- an enum: the Rust enum or newtype that stands in for it, and each of its constants: the
  variant or the constant that stands in for it.
- a macro: the generic, `const`, function or `macro_rules!` that stands in for it; a type
  generator's instances keep their own kinds, on the aliases.
- a function pointer: the callable type that stands in for it, or the trait, for a struct
  of function pointers.
- a typedef: the alias that stands in for it.
- a member: each of its accessors, the getter and the setter alike.
### 3.2 Several stand-ins
One C item may have several annotated Rust items, each carrying the same anchor and
alias: the ownership variants one C function is split into when one signature cannot
express every valid contract, as [`binding-symbols`](../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s
Functions section describes, and the accessors of one field. That is the only case in which an
annotation is duplicated. Existing annotations are completed work unless the current
objective deliberately promotes their item: a port of an item a binding wraps, or the
`port/layout` that gives a wrapped struct or union its native layout, replaces its `Wraps`
anchor with a `Replaces` one, and keeps its alias.
## 4. Testing
Tests are placed by what they target. Tests of the public interface are Cargo integration
tests of the safe crate, under `tests/`, so crate privacy enforces
the public-interface boundary. Each suite's `main.rs` declares one module per tested
translation unit, in `<suite>/<the tested TU>.rs`.
- Tests that target undefined behaviour on the safe public interface are placed in
  `tests/ub_safe`, whose `main.rs` carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`. Those the compiler
  should reject are placed in `tests/ub_safe/compile_fail/`.
- Tests that target undefined behaviour on the unsafe public interface are placed in
  `tests/ub_unsafe`.
- Tests that compare the module's exported API with C's are placed in `tests/equiv_pub`,
  and those that compare its internals with C's in an inline `#[cfg(test)] mod equiv_priv`
  beside the unit they test.
- Tests that check the public interface through Rust assertions are placed in
  `tests/unit_pub`, and those that check internal routines in an inline
  `#[cfg(test)] mod unit_priv` beside the unit they test.
An inline test of a region's code sits in that region, and an inline test that holds
unsafe code, such as an `equiv_priv` test calling the C, sits in a region: the module's
`ffi_import`, for the C it calls. The suites whose tests call the raw bindings or the public unsafe API,
`tests/ub_unsafe` and `tests/equiv_pub`, take `unsafe_code` back at their `main.rs`, as a
region does.
A standalone reproducer is not a test: it is placed with the report that cites it.

---
name: conventions
description: "Naming, tree layout, anchors and test placement of the Rust a campaign generates. Read before writing, homing or reviewing generated Rust or tests."
---
# Crustify coding conventions
These are the shared, mechanical contracts of the code a campaign generates: how it is
named, where it sits, how it records what it translated and where its tests go. The
toolchain, edition, lints and formatting it is held to are [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s.
## 1. Naming
The workspace's lints enforce the standard Rust casing below, as [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s
Lints section describes.
The safe surface uses ordinary Rust naming: `snake_case` for functions, methods and
modules, `UpperCamelCase` for types and traits, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` for constants and
statics. A C name's library or owning-type prefix is dropped wherever the crate, module or
receiver already supplies it, and the idiomatic Rust term is preferred over a
transliterated C one. The filled anchor records the C name, so renaming costs no
traceability. Names that cross the language boundary keep their C-derived spelling, as
below.
### 1.1 Functions
A C function's raw binding is `sys::<name>`. Its safe wrapper is a free function homed in
the owning module, named by the rules above. When one C function has several valid
ownership contracts, each safe variant has a distinct, descriptive name.
### 1.2 Types
A wrapped C type is the layout-compatible newtype `Foo`, named by the rules above; its
shared and exclusive borrowed handles are `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`, and its sole and
counted owners `FooBox` and `FooArc`. A port keeps these names while what they name
changes, as [`porting-types`](../porting/types/SKILL.md)'s Structs section describes. A typedef that
names a type under another name, which its item lists among its `typedefs`, is a
`pub type` alias of the type's Rust form.
A function pointer a typedef declares is named after its typedef. One written inline is
named after the site that declares it, its holder's name followed by its own and `Fn`: a
field's `<Struct><Field>Fn`, a parameter's `<Function><Param>Fn`, a return's
`<Function>ReturnFn` and a global's `<Global>Fn`.
### 1.3 Shims
A callable macro shim is `crustify_<NAME>`.
### 1.4 Exports
Each ported module has one raw ABI gateway, its `ffi_export` region, as
[Unsafe regions](#21-unsafe-regions) describes, whose exports use `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] extern "C"` under the bare C names: the
module's functions and globals that C outside the module references, another module's TU
or a C test or executable that stays, the `static inline` functions its headers define
included. The exports serve that C, which reaches the module through them once it has
switched. A function or global only the module's own C references is not exported: that
C leaves the build with the module at its switch, and its callers are Rust from then
on; nor are static functions and static globals, which nothing outside their TU reaches.
The target's public C API, for C outside the target, is deferred: exports serve the
target's own remaining C alone, and that API is a layer of its own over the native Rust API,
added once the modules it covers are ported.
<!-- TODO: that layer, a C-compatible ABI over the ported public API, is not specified
yet. Until it is, a C consumer outside the target does not survive a port. -->
An export is removed, with the raw binding that reaches it, by its symbol's `port/unexport`,
after the switch that removes the last C that calls it, takes its address or
accesses it. A C test tied to the module that stays, using only its public API, does not
hold an export back: it checks the export while other C needs it, and leaves with it.
### 1.5 Export features
Each module's `ffi_export` is compiled only under the safe crate's Cargo feature
`ffi-export-<tu>`, with `<tu>` its translation unit's path below the C root, every character
that is not an ASCII letter or digit replaced by `-`. The feature is off until the module
switches, so that its exports never collide with the C they replace, and the switch
deletes it, its gateway compiling unconditionally from then on.
## 2. Crates, modules, and TUs
The Rust tree is the repository's own, as [`layout`](../../operations/layout/SKILL.md)'s Tree section lays it
out, all relative to the repository's root:
- `Cargo.toml` - the safe crate's manifest, which also declares the workspace.
- `src/lib.rs` - the safe crate's root, with one `cfg`-gated module per link unit.
- `src/<link-unit>/` - one sub-dir per link unit.
- `src/sys.rs` and `sys/<link-unit>/` - the raw bindings, one public module per link unit,
  laid out as [`bindgen`](../bindgen/SKILL.md) describes.
The safe crate is named after its repository, `<repo>-crustify`, as
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Repositories section names it:
a name crates.io leaves free, which tells it apart from the source's own Rust bindings,
such as `git2` for libgit2.
Within a link unit's sub-dir, the tree follows the module decomposition in `modules.json`
exactly, and preserves the C layout as far as the idiomatic organization of a Rust tree
allows:
- each module is one `.rs` file, at its translation unit's path below the C root with the
  `.rs` extension: its TU and the headers bundled with it have no files of their own,
  since Rust has no headers;
- a header module is one `<stem>_h.rs` file, at its header's path;
- the two modules of a split foundational TU share the TU's file;
- C directories become Rust modules: a directory's `.rs` file sits beside the directory,
  as `<dir>.rs` and `<dir>/`, and declares the modules within it, or is the module of a TU
  with the directory's name where there is one; `mod.rs` files are not used; and
- a file or directory name that is not a Rust identifier is sanitized, hyphens to
  underscores, and a Rust keyword takes a trailing underscore.
Where a C layout has no idiomatic Rust counterpart, the tree adapts it in the conventional
Rust way and keeps the C path recognizable. A batch names the `.rs` file each of its items
belongs in, as `src/<link-unit>/…/<file>.rs`. Entities sharing a
definition site co-home. A home may be shared across waves.
### 2.1 Unsafe regions
A module's unsafe code is confined to at most two inline child modules of its file, its
unsafe regions, so that the rest of the file, its native code, holds none:
- `mod ffi_import`: what the module reaches in C: its calls through the raw bindings, the C
  layouts it wraps with their handles and accessors, the owners and lifecycle policies over
  C's allocator, and the trampolines and contexts through which C calls a Rust closure
  back; and
- `mod ffi_export { use super::*; … }`: the gateway through which C reaches the module by
  symbol, as [Exports](#14-exports) describes, compiled only under its
  [export feature](#15-export-features).
Unsafe code is every `unsafe` block, `unsafe fn`, `unsafe impl`, `unsafe extern` block and
`#[unsafe(…)]` attribute, and every invocation of another crate's macro that expands to
one, such as one that mints a type over a C layout, which the compiler's `unsafe_code` lint does not
see. Outside the regions, only the raw bindings hold any. The regions take the lint back as
[`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Unsafe code section describes.
A region exposes to its module only what [`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary
section lets it expose, and the module re-exports the public items a region defines, as
`pub use ffi_import::{Foo, FooBox, FooMut, FooRef};`, so that their paths do not depend on
which side defines them. A type's inherent `impl` blocks may be split between the native
code and a region: each method is visible as its own visibility says, counted from the
module that holds its block, so that a region's private helpers stay hidden from the
native code.
A region exists only while it holds something. A wrap's items are in `ffi_import`. A port
writes its item in the native code, and keeps in the regions only the C form the item
keeps, as [`porting`](../porting/SKILL.md) describes; a wrapped item it ports leaves
`ffi_import` with its re-export. The later stages empty the regions part by part: an
item's C layout and C owners leave `ffi_import` with its `port/layout` and `port/memory`,
its export leaves `ffi_export` with its `port/unexport`. A module without either region is
native, and its file carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`.
## 3. Anchors
The Rust item that stands in for each C item is annotated, and those annotations are the
only record that an item was translated.
An annotation is two attributes on the same Rust item, a doc-comment anchor and a rustdoc
alias:
```rust
/// Wraps `fn::git_repository_open`
#[doc(alias = "git_repository_open")]
pub fn open(path: &Path) -> Result<RepositoryBox, Error> { … }
```
| anchor | meaning |
|---|---|
| ``/// Wraps `<kind>::<path>` `` | safe view over the FFI seam |
| ``/// Replaces `<kind>::<path>` `` | native Rust translation |
The anchor's path is a code span, in backticks, as rustdoc renders it and as the
workspace's `clippy::doc_markdown` lint requires of a path in a doc comment.
`<path>` names the item as its batch schedules it, and `<kind>` says what it is:
| kind | item |
|---|---|
| `fn` | a function |
| `st` | a struct |
| `un` | a union |
| `enm` | an enum, or one of its constants |
| `fnp` | a function pointer |
| `tdf` | a typedef: one of its own, or one an item lists among its `typedefs` |
| `fld` | a member of a struct or union |
| `glb` | a global |
| `mac` | a macro |
A path is made of names only: the names the source resolves the item by, outermost first,
separated by `.`, as the source language scopes them. A function, a type, an enum's
constant, a global, a typedef or a function pointer a typedef declares is its own name,
since C scopes a constant as it does its enum. A member is its struct's or union's path
followed by the member's name, and a member of a member continues the path, as
`fld::AVOption.default_val.i64`. A function pointer written inline is its declaring site's
path: a member's, `<function>.<param>` for a parameter, `<function>.return` for a return,
or a global's name. An element without a name adds no step to the paths of what it holds:
- an anonymous struct or union held by a named member is reached through that member, so
  its members are `fld::<path>.<member>.<inner>`;
- the members of an unnamed struct or union member, such as C11's anonymous members, are
  named as members of the type that holds it, as the source reaches them; and
- an array's elements are reached without an index, so the members of an array member's
  element type are `fld::<path>.<member>.<inner>`.
An element without a name has no annotation of its own. The Rust item that stands in for
it is annotated with the named member that holds it, or, when it is held by no name, with
each member it stands in for. A type declared inside another is named as its language
scopes it: a C struct tag has file scope, so a struct declared inside another is still
`st::<tag>`. An enum without a name has no annotation of its own, and its constants keep
theirs.
The alias is the bare `<path>`, without the backticks, so that a consumer who searches the
documentation for the source's name finds every item that stands in for it. The kind is
the anchor's alone: a label in the alias would no longer match that search.
### 3.1 What is annotated
The annotation goes on the public item a consumer uses in place of the C item, which is
not necessarily the item that makes the FFI call:
- a function: the function or method the public API exports, which a consumer imports
  instead of the FFI function. The private helper that makes the call, an `ffi_export`
  gateway and a test are not annotated.
- a lifecycle routine, raw, typed or string: the method of the public lifecycle trait the
  strategy implements, such as `CDrop::c_drop`, where it is handwritten, or the macro
  invocation that mints it, which passes the annotation to the method. Again, the method
  annotated need not be the one making the unsafe call.
- a type: the layout newtype that defines the FFI type, handwritten or minted by
  `define_ctype!`.
- a union: the tagged enum that stands in for it at every use.
- an enum: the Rust enum or newtype that stands in for it, and each of its constants: the
  variant or the constant that stands in for it.
- a macro: the generic, `const`, function or `macro_rules!` that stands in for it; a type
  generator's instances keep their own kinds, on the aliases.
- a function pointer: the callable type that stands in for it, or the trait, for a struct
  of function pointers.
- a typedef: the alias that stands in for it.
- a member: each of its accessors, the getter and the setter alike.
### 3.2 Several stand-ins
One C item may have several annotated Rust items, each carrying the same anchor and
alias: the ownership variants one C function is split into when one signature cannot
express every valid contract, as [`binding-symbols`](../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s
Functions section describes, and the accessors of one field. That is the only case in which an
annotation is duplicated. Existing annotations are completed work unless the current
objective deliberately promotes their item: a port of an item a binding wraps, or the
`port/layout` that gives a wrapped struct or union its native layout, replaces its `Wraps`
anchor with a `Replaces` one, and keeps its alias.
## 4. Testing
Tests are placed by what they target. Tests of the public interface are Cargo integration
tests of the safe crate, under `tests/`, so crate privacy enforces
the public-interface boundary. Each suite's `main.rs` declares one module per tested
translation unit, in `<suite>/<the tested TU>.rs`.
- Tests that target undefined behaviour on the safe public interface are placed in
  `tests/ub_safe`, whose `main.rs` carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`. Those the compiler
  should reject are placed in `tests/ub_safe/compile_fail/`.
- Tests that target undefined behaviour on the unsafe public interface are placed in
  `tests/ub_unsafe`.
- Tests that compare the module's exported API with C's are placed in `tests/equiv_pub`,
  and those that compare its internals with C's in an inline `#[cfg(test)] mod equiv_priv`
  beside the unit they test.
- Tests that check the public interface through Rust assertions are placed in
  `tests/unit_pub`, and those that check internal routines in an inline
  `#[cfg(test)] mod unit_priv` beside the unit they test.
An inline test of a region's code sits in that region, and an inline test that holds
unsafe code, such as an `equiv_priv` test calling the C, sits in a region: the module's
`ffi_import`, for the C it calls. The suites whose tests call the raw bindings or the public unsafe API,
`tests/ub_unsafe` and `tests/equiv_pub`, take `unsafe_code` back at their `main.rs`, as a
region does.
A standalone reproducer is not a test: it is placed with the report that cites it.

---
name: evolution
description: "How Crustify repairs and improves itself from what its campaigns expose: goals, signals, proposals, lessons, evolution branches, validation, review, autonomy, adoption, the record of what landed and how evolution itself evolves. Read before filing a defect in Crustify or a tool, proposing or making a change to either, or recording a campaign's lesson."
---

# Evolution

How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as
its `PROPOSAL.md`: the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it
cites; its destination; the change, or the patch; how it was validated; its review's
verdict; and its status, `open`, `landed`, with the commit it landed as, or `declined`,
with why. A lesson is not
filed as a proposal: `LESSONS.md` records it.

A defect in a tool found while reviewing is such a proposal, not a finding on the reviewed
code, and is filed with its reproducer.

## 5. Lessons

The campaign's lessons sit in `crustify/LESSONS.md`, read by every run of the campaign
before its first step. Each is one rule, with the evidence it rests on and its scope, the
modules, items or stages it holds for. A lesson a second campaign records again is
generalized into the spec, by a proposal citing both.

## 6. Changes

A campaign evolves each component, Crustify or a tool, on a working branch of its own in
that component's repository, `<campaign-id>/devel`, the campaign id being the name of the
campaign's repository. It is forked from the component's `devel` when the campaign first
needs it, and the campaign's runs read and run the component from its checkout, so that a
campaign runs on what it has changed and no other campaign does.

A change is made on a branch named `<campaign-id>/evolution/<slug>`, forked from that
working branch, in a worktree beside the repository that lives only while the change is
made. A branch holds one concern. Once the change lands on the working branch, by a
fast-forward, the worktree is purged and the branch deleted. Its commits take the identity
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives the
campaign's.

- A change to the spec follows `authoring`: written once, in the place its kind belongs,
  as generally as the evidence allows.
- A change to what a tool does comes with a regression test: the reproducer of a defect
  becomes one, and a new behaviour gets one that fails without it. A change to its
  documentation alone adds none, unless the defect it fixes has a reproducer, which becomes
  a test or a doctest. A packaging defect's reproducer becomes a test too, run
  against a build installed as a dependent installs it. The tool's whole suite passes, its
  opt-in tests included wherever the change touches what they cover.
- A new tool is drafted and tested where it serves a repeated procedure, preferably as a
  subcommand of an existing tool within that tool's goals, or as a script in the skill
  that describes its use, as `authoring` places one; a tool of its own repository is
  merged upstream only with the user's approval.

A fix that unblocks the campaign, or that would prevent a defect in later campaigns, is
landed on the working branch as soon as it is reviewed, rather than batched.

## 7. Validation

A tool's change is validated by its tests, the regression test it adds among them.

A spec change that a failure prompted is validated by running again what failed, the item,
the batch or the stage, under the change: a lightweight run, without the tests or gates
the failure does not need to show. The proposal records what the run produced before and
after, and a change whose rerun still fails does not land. A spec change no failure
prompted, such as a rule loosened or a waste removed, is validated the same way where its
effect is in doubt, on the item its evidence came from.

A rerun shows that a change answers the case that exposed it, not that it holds: that is
watched in the campaigns after it lands, as [Record](#11-record) describes.

## 8. Review

Every change is reviewed before it lands, on its evolution branch, by a run other than the
one that made it. The review reads the proposal, the change and its validation, and checks
that:

- the proposal's evidence shows the signal, and the change answers it;
- the change serves a goal, and a tool's stays within the tool's own goals;
- it is placed and written as [`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md) describes, and states
  no rule in the target's names;
- its validation was run, and shows what the proposal says;
- its entry of [Record](#11-record), which the change or its proposal drafts, names a
  recurrence signal a campaign would observe, and `test` only where its test checks all of
  it; and
- whether it weakens a check, which the verdict marks.

A review runs under the campaign's working branch of the component, never under the change
it reviews, and reads the change from its branch. Its task pins the commit it reviews, and
only that commit lands, by a fast-forward of the working branch: a commit added after the
verdict, or one a rebase or cherry-pick makes, is reviewed again. Its checks are this section's and its
role's; the task message of the run that asks for it adds to them, and never relaxes them.
A review reads as deeply as the change reaches: a change to documentation alone is read; a
tool's code, a check, a soundness fix and every rule of the spec are reviewed with their
validation run again.

The verdict is recorded in the proposal's Review section, approved or rejected, with its
reasons; a rejection leaves the proposal open for another change or for the user.

What only records what was decided, a status of [Record](#11-record) a check changes or a
proposal's status, verdict and review, changes no rule and is not reviewed; an entry is
reviewed with its change.

A change that weakens a check, a gate, a test, a lint, a review objective, a tool's
detection or a rule of this skill, is marked so in the verdict and in its entry of the
record, since a run that can loosen what judges it passes by loosening it: the user reads
each such change on its own before `devel` takes it, as [Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.

## 9. Autonomy

The settings' `evolution` answer sets how far a campaign evolves the harness:

| answer | what lands on the campaign's working branches |
|---|---|
| `off` | nothing: no proposal, no lesson |

# Evolution

How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as
its `PROPOSAL.md`: the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it
cites; its destination; the change, or the patch; how it was validated; its review's
verdict; and its status, `open`, `landed`, with the commit it landed as, or `declined`,
with why. A lesson is not

code, and is filed with its reproducer.

The campaign's lessons sit in `crustify/LESSONS.md`, read by every run of the campaign
before its first step. Each is one rule, with the evidence it rests on and its scope, the
modules, items or stages it holds for. A lesson a second campaign records again is
generalized into the spec, by a proposal citing both.

that component's repository, `<campaign-id>/devel`, the campaign id being the name of the
campaign's repository. It is forked from the component's `devel` when the campaign first
needs it, and the campaign's runs read and run the component from its checkout, so that a
campaign runs on what it has changed and no other campaign does.
